paper_title: MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The last mile toward enterprise AGI is a company that runs itself. Training and adapting such agents require longitudinal enterprise data, which remain scarce, costly to acquire, and often restricted by privacy constraints. Historical archives are also frequently incomplete and record only what actually happened. They cannot show the outcomes of alternative decisions. We introduce MiniCorp, an office simulator for studying how agents can collectively run a company while generating enterprise data at scale. Using an e-commerce company as a demonstration, MiniCorp connects two interacting worlds. The external world models customers, dynamic competitors, and market mechanisms. The internal world consists of agents that observe events, discuss their options, and make strategic decisions. These decisions have lasting effects on the market, and the resulting feedback informs the firm's later decisions. As the firm and market interact, MiniCorp continuously records the agents' communications and decisions. These records preserve the information available at the time and the business results that followed. Checkpointing allows the same situation to be replayed under different decisions, providing comparisons unavailable in static archives. We evaluate end-to-end fidelity against patterns reported in empirical studies of real markets. These evaluations provide agents with realistic market feedback and reduce the risk that they learn to exploit flaws in the simulator. Our experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting their decisions to market feedback. With explicit long-term strategic guidance, they also sustain advertising exploration despite weak early returns. MiniCorp thus provides an environment for studying AI-run companies and a scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation.

sections.content: MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm Jingying Zeng1*, Zhenwei Dai1*, Jinning Li2, Changho Shin3, Dylan Zhang2, Yuxuan Lu4, Qi He1, Dakuo Wang4, Kai-Wei Chang5 1 Microsoft, 2 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, 3 Princeton University, 4 Northeastern University, 5 UCLA (cid:128) Website: https://agents-minicorp.com/ Abstract The last mile toward enterprise AGI is company that runs itself. Training and adapting such agents require longitudinal enterprise data, which remain scarce, costly to acquire, and often restricted by privacy constraints. Historical archives are also frequently incomplete and record only what actually happened. They cannot show the outcomes of alternative decisions. We introduce MiniCorp, an office simulator for studying how agents can collectively run company while generating enterprise data at scale. Using an e-commerce company as demonstration, MiniCorp connects two interacting worlds. The external world models customers, dynamic competitors, and market mechanisms. The internal world consists of agents that observe events, discuss their options, and make strategic decisions. These decisions have lasting effects on the market, and the resulting feedback informs the firms later decisions. As the firm and market interact, MiniCorp continuously records the agents communications and decisions. These records preserve the information available at the time and the business results that followed. Checkpointing allows the same situation to be replayed under different decisions, providing comparisons unavailable in static archives. We evaluate end-to-end fidelity against patterns reported in empirical studies of real markets. These evaluations provide agents with realistic market feedback and reduce the risk that they learn to exploit flaws in the simulator. Our experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting their decisions to market feedback. With explicit long-term strategic guidance, they also sustain advertising exploration despite weak early returns. MiniCorp thus provides an environment for studying AI-run companies and scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation. Figure 1: The simulated e-commerce environment where autonomous agent-run company is interacting with an exogenous external world. *Equal contribution. 1 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm 1. Introduction From chatbots to long-running agents, the path toward AGI can be viewed as unfolding in stages: (i) the chatbot: systems that answer questions; (ii) the autonomous agent: systems that act, using tools, operating software, and completing long-horizon tasks end to end; and (iii) organizational autonomy: the capacity of system of agents to go beyond the tasks handed to them and collectively run an organization by setting strategic direction, making business decisions under uncertainty, coordinating work across roles, and keeping the organization alive and profitable over time. In the enterprise setting, this progression points toward company that can run itself. We view such company as the last mile toward enterprise AGI. Existing agents, however, are primarily designed to complete assigned tasks, rather than persist as an organization that sets its own priorities and coordinates decisions across roles in pursuit of long-term profitability. The limitations of task-oriented agents become especially apparent in business operations, an economically consequential domain in which decisions are complex, context-dependent, and evaluated through consequences that unfold over time. Unlike many coding or mathematical tasks, for which correctness can often be evaluated against tests or predefined answers, business decisions rarely have single correct action that can be verified in advance. Their consequences emerge through interactions among the firm, customers, competitors, and market conditions, and may not become fully observable for months or even years. Training, adapting, and evaluating agents capable of running business therefore requires longitudinal enterprise data that connects decisions to their business context and downstream consequences. Such data are exceptionally scarce because the most valuable records are internal and often unavailable for training due to privacy and compliance constraints. Archives from bankrupt firms can provide genuine enterprise data, but acquiring proprietary collections can be expensive. For example, Google was selected as the winning bidder in bankruptcy auction with $10 million offer for Spirit Airlines internal business data, including employee emails, Microsoft Teams messages, spreadsheets, calendars, and operational records, which it planned to use for product development and AI training.1 Such archives are valuable because they preserve authentic organizational communications and documented business decisions. However, they remain limited in two important ways. First, records from bankrupt firms and publicly available corpora, such as the Enron corpus2 [Klimt and Yang, 2004], are often fragmented and do not provide the full context needed to reconstruct the circumstances in which recorded decisions were made. Missing context may include the state of the firm and its market, the information available to each role, preceding communications, resource constraints, and the outcomes that followed. Second, historical archives are frozen: they contain only the decisions that were actually made and the single trajectory that followed. As result, they cannot answer counterfactual what if questions because the outcomes of alternative decisions are unobserved. Such archives are therefore insufficient on their own for interactive reinforcement learning, which requires agents to take alternative actions and observe their consequences. Existing agent benchmarks, including τ2-Bench [Barres et al., 2025], SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2024], GAIA [Mialon et al., 2024], and OSWorld [Xie et al., 2024], primarily evaluate agents on bounded tasks with predefined objectives and verifiable outcomes, rather than requiring them to operate company continuously within an evolving market. Running company instead requires agents to act over extended periods, make decisions without single correct action specified in advance, coordinate through persistent organizational roles, and adapt to the lasting effects of earlier decisions. Long1Yahoo Finance report 2https://www.cs.cmu.edu/enron/ 2 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm horizon environments have also been developed for multi-agent social simulation [Akkil et al., 2026] and single-agent business operation with pre-defined market events, including MerchantBench [Shi et al., 2026] and EnterpriseArena [Han et al., 2026]. Even when multiple agents appear in existing benchmarks, they are typically assembled around particular task and cease to matter once it is completed. What is therefore missing is checkpointable office simulator that combines persistent organization with an evolving external market, allowing the two to co-evolve and generate longitudinal enterprise data that connect organizational decisions to their changing context and downstream consequences, while supporting replay under alternative decisions. MiniCorp addresses these gaps by instantiating office simulations that couple two interacting worlds: an evolving external market and persistent agent firm. Using e-commerce as demonstration (Figure 2), the external world consists of customers, adaptive competitors, suppliers, marketplace platforms, and the macroeconomic conditions under which they operate. The internal world provides persistent organizational structure: standing roles communicate, coordinate, and retain their responsibilities across decision cycles, rather than being created temporarily for individual tasks. The evolving external world captures long-horizon consequences by continuing to operate whether or not the agent firm acts, allowing earlier decisions to produce delayed and lasting market effects. Their closed-loop interaction supports the generation of contextual and counterfactual enterprise data: market events and status flow into the agent firm, agent firm decisions alter the external world, and the resulting outcomes become the next round of observations. Checkpointing further allows the same state to be replayed under alternative decisions. Finally, MiniCorp addresses the challenge of simulating realistic market responses by explicitly modeling the inspectable operational pathways through which business decisions generate market outcomes. For example, simulated customer submits search query, receives results page containing sponsored and organic listings, chooses whether to click product, and then decides whether to purchase it. Modeling this pathway requires explicit mechanisms for queryproduct matching and ranking, sponsored-search auctions, click-through behavior, and conversion behavior. We ground these components in empirical research and real marketplace data, while adapting broader business mechanisms from Capitalism II3, commercial business-simulation engine whose events and economic logic have been tuned over years of play. Because these enterprise records are generated through simulated market interactions, their usefulness depends critically on the fidelity of the external world. Fidelity evaluation is therefore central not only to assessing the validity of the simulated external world, but also to guiding the simulators continued refinement. Realistic-looking market snapshots and exact numerical alignment are not sufficient because market conditions and numerical magnitudes vary across products, firms, platforms, and time periods. In principle, high-fidelity external-world simulator should support the range of business decisions available to human-operated firm in the represented setting and provide corresponding market feedback. For each such decision, the resulting market response should be consistent with empirical evidence in three respects: its direction and temporal dynamics, how it distributes gains and losses among market participants, and whether improving one business outcome comes at the expense of another. Moreover, the simulator should reproduce not only the final outcomes of decisions but also the intermediate response pathways through which those outcomes arise. Otherwise, agents may learn simulator-specific regularities that do not transfer to real markets, failure mode we refer to as simulator overfitting. Fidelity must therefore be evaluated at the system level because individually grounded mechanisms for ranking, advertising, pricing, and inventory may interact through feedback loops and produce unrealistic behavior when combined. We evaluate the integrated external world 3https://store.steampowered.com/app/638200/Capitalism_2/ 3 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm end-to-end against multiple empirical response patterns and use the resulting evidence to identify missing or incorrect response pathways that require further refinement (Section 3.5). In this work, our key contributions are: MiniCorp, closed-loop office simulator with an empirically evaluated external world. MiniCorp couples an evolving external market with persistent agent firm, producing continuous streams of enterprise data that connect organizational communications and decisions to their market consequences. Using e-commerce as demonstration, we present general approach to constructing industry-specific external worlds by integrating established economic mechanisms, empirical evidence, and real-world data into explicit market processes with adaptive participants. We further provide methodology for evaluating end-to-end fidelity, together with experimental evidence that the integrated external world produces market-response patterns consistent with empirical studies. scalable and efficient enterprise data engine. Because the company runs continuously, it leaves behind the record real company leaves behind (message, email, meetings, tickets, documents, etc) at volume and speed no privacy-constrained corpus can match, with full provenance linking every artifact to the market state and the decision that produced it. Because its state is checkpointable, the same situation can be replayed under different decisions, yielding the counterfactual pairs static archive cannot supply. 2. Related Works Social simulation. large body of work uses LLM agents to simulate people, taking human-likeness as the objective and emergent collective behavior as the finding. The research on generative agents was pioneered by Stanfords Smallville [Park et al., 2023], sandbox town of 25 agents with memory, reflection, and planning, where individual emergent behavior gave rise to unscripted information diffusion and social coordination. Subsequent work extends this along two axes. The first is persona fidelity and breadth: agents grounded in two-hour interviews with 1,052 Americans recover their survey responses at roughly 85% of the participants own testretest consistency [Park et al., 2024], and MatrAIx [Li et al., 2026] scales persona construction to 8.3 billion records across 1,290 dimensions. The second is horizon and consequence: Emergence World [Akkil et al., 2026] runs continuous world for weeks under persistent memory and self-governance with irreversible consequences, where the model backbone alone separates stable governance from population collapsemaking safety an ecosystem rather than model property. In all of these the referent is human and success means human-likeness. Office work and company operation benchmarks Existing workplace benchmarks trade off environment fidelity and task horizon, and most resolve that tension by shrinking the horizon until company becomes task. ChatDev [Qian et al., 2024] and The Virtual Biotech [Zhang et al., 2026] borrow firms org chart as coordination scaffold to measure agents end-to-end completion of bounded tasks with verifiable signal. EnterpriseBench [Vishwakarma et al., 2025], Workflow-GYM [Zhu et al., 2026], and MultiAgentBench [Zhu et al., 2025] widen the environment to enterprise data, professional GUIs, and multi-agent coordination, yet still terminate at task boundary. GDPval [Patwardhan et al., 2026] and APEX-Agents [Vidgen et al., 2026] push the fidelity axis to its limit by sourcing tasks from real occupations and grading against human expert deliverable quality, but each case remains single bounded deliverable, evaluated in isolation with no persistent firm, evolving world, or economic ledger. second group restores the horizon and hard economic signal: FoodTruckBench [foo, 2026] and MerchantBench [Shi et al., 2026] run business for month to year and score final net worth, but the agent is lone operator acting on small hand-authored world model. Closest to us, TheAgent4 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm Company [Xu et al., 2025] and EnterpriseArena [Han et al., 2026] target company operation itself, one through self-hosted software stack with scripted colleagues, the other through 132 months of survival inside an abstract financial model. 3. Problem Statement and Methods MiniCorp models business operation as closed-loop interaction between two stateful systems: an external world and an internal agent firm (Figure 2). At high level, the external world consists of consumers, dynamic competitors, suppliers, an e-commerce platform whose explicit market mechanisms support the business decisions available to human-operated firm and generate corresponding market feedback, and the broader macroeconomic conditions under which they interact. Explicit market mechanisms connect the firms business actions to outcomes such as search visibility, customer demand, sales, inventory movement, and competitor responses. The internal world is an AI agent firm composed of organizational roles with different responsibilities and access to information. In each simulation cycle, market events and status become observations for these roles, while their approved decisions are executed in the external world and alter its state. The resulting outcomes provide the next round of observations, allowing the market and the agent firm to evolve together over time. For given industry, MiniCorp constructs an external world that makes two core dimensions of firm capability observable: strategic capability and long-term vision. Together, these dimensions capture whether newly founded agent firm can build business from scratch and operate it effectively over time. We use e-commerce as running example to show how these capabilities are instantiated through carefully selected decision settings and to illustrate general approach for constructing, evaluating, and iteratively refining an external world so that it more closely approximates the real setting it represents. For instance, in e-commerce, advertising and pricing decisions provide particularly clear setting in which both dimensions come into play. Effective advertising requires strategic capability because firms must discover valuable search queries, interpret performance feedback, adjust bids, allocate budgets, and control acquisition costs. It also requires long-term vision because firms must balance immediate paid sales against potential improvements in future organic visibility. Figure 2: Overview of MiniCorps interaction between the external world model and the internal AI agent team for an autonomous e-commerce company. 5 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm 3.1. The External World Model The external world is an autonomous economy. The key departure of this evolving eternal world from task-oriented benchmarks is that the world is not task interface but self-advancing economy. It runs whether or not the firm acts. Shocks fire, in-flight orders arrive, competitors move, and demand shifts across categories, with no action from the agent firm. The simulation models represent the consumers, suppliers, logistics providers, competitors and platform that firm trades with, together with the macroeconomic conditions they sit in. Competitors also react to what the agent firm does. price cut can be matched, and quality advantage can be narrowed. Let Wt denote the external world state at period t. The state is cumulative rather than snapshot. Inventory, product standing, supplier reputation and undelivered purchase orders all persist, so consequence incurred in one period is still present many periods later. The transition is parameterized by latent structural parameters Λ that the agent firm never observes, such as consumer preference weights over price and quality, or suppliers true defect propensity. Let be the catalogue of available decisions and Dt the decisions taken in period t, and let Zt be an exogenous process carrying the macroeconomic regime and shocks such as tariff changes and freight-rate spikes. The world evolves according to Wt+1 PΛ( Wt, Dt, Zt) , where PΛ is the conditional distribution of the next state given the current state, the agent firms decisions, and exogenous events. (1) We adapt several economic mechanisms documented for Capitalism II, including how consumers choose among competing products. Each product category has limited amount of demand. Our firms products and rival products compete for that demand. The simulator evaluates all of these products using the same scoring rules. The demand is then divided according to those scores. Each category weights price, quality and brand differently, so buyers of one product type may care mostly about price while buyers of another care mostly about quality. The same price cut therefore moves demand by different amounts depending on the category product sits in. The engine supplies default weights, and each world draws its own values near them. Those values go into Λ, so the agent firm cannot look up what its buyers care about. It has to infer that from how the market responds. The second source is published evidence from real markets. It fixes the mechanisms and parameter ranges the engine does not determine, including tariff pass-through, supplier lead times and defect rates. Where the evidence supports range rather than single value, the parameter is sampled once at world initialization and held fixed for the run. 3.2. Constructing the E-Commerce Competition World We construct synthetic e-commerce platform that explicitly represents the major marketplace processes through which business decisions affect outcomes. Because MiniCorp models the complete downstream response to business decision, it cannot map an action directly to sales or profit while omitting the intermediate mechanisms. We therefore simulate search demand, querylisting matching, organic search ranking, search-results pages, click and conversion behavior for each querystock-keeping-unit (SKU) pair, sponsored-search auctions, and competitor responses. Together, these components form an explicit response chain from firms decision to consumer behavior, sales, future search visibility, and subsequent competitive actions. Preserving these intermediate processes is necessary both for the fidelity of the simulated external world and for evaluating the stratigic capability and long-term vision of an agent firm. An experienced 6 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm firm does not reason only from terminal revenue or profit. It diagnoses whether performance is constrained by insufficient impressions, low click-through rates, weak conversion, high advertising costs, or competitor actions, and then intervenes at the appropriate stage. To represent this decision process, MiniCorp models the following marketplace components. (I) Search demand. Search demand forms the first layer of the marketplace because it determines the opportunities over which listings compete. We construct base set of 1,000 search queries [Everaert et al., 2024]: 316 relatively common queries collected from Amazon autocomplete and 684 more specific long-tail queries constructed from attributes of products in the simulated marketplace. This combination preserves the language of real searches while ensuring that long-tail queries can distinguish among products in the smaller simulated product catalog. The autocomplete ordering places relatively common terms near the head of the distribution, while the constructed queries form its long tail. We then use Zipf law to assign more search traffic to head queries and progressively less traffic to long-tail queries. We use ESCI examples [Reddy et al., 2022] as few-shot demonstrations for an LLM that classifies the relevance of each product category to each query as exact, substitute, complementary, or irrelevant. These labels determine which product categories may appear in the results for each query. At the weekly horizon, aggregate query demand is treated as external to any individual seller. Category conditions, calendar effects, and other market-level factors may change how frequently consumers search, while sellers compete over which listings receive and convert the resulting traffic. (II) Products and listings. Products and listings define the alternatives available to consumers for each search query. Each SKU has product category and observable specifications, such as device compatibility, power, battery capacity, connector and port configuration, and product form factor. Each marketplace listing further associates the SKU with seller, title, brand, price, age, product quality, cost structure, delivery conditions, rating distribution, and review history. These attributes are used consistently by the matching, ranking, click, and conversion models. To initialize incumbent sellers with operating histories, we run 26-week warm-up period before the agent firm enters. During this period, rival sellers compete for organic and sponsored traffic and adjust their pricing and advertising strategies. We carry the resulting query-level sales histories, sales velocities, advertising states, and recent auction clearing prices into the external worlds initial state. Accumulated sales are also used to initialize reviews. We refer to the resulting state as simulator-generated prehistory. The agent firm therefore enters an operating marketplace whose incumbents already have the histories required by the ranking and competitor models. (III) Search matching and ranking. The search engine transforms query demand into organic visibility through separate matching and ranking stages. The matching stage first removes irrelevant listings and evaluates whether each remaining listings title and product specifications satisfy the requirements expressed in the query. The organic ranking stage then orders the eligible listings using three groups of signals: behavioral evidence, including query-level click-through rate, conversion rate, and recent sales velocity; querylisting relevance and specification match; and offer characteristics, including price, product quality, brand, delivery, and reviews. The resulting order determines which listings appear on each search-results page and how many organic impressions they receive. 7 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm (IV) Click and conversion. Click-through and conversion models represent the next two stages of consumer response. Click-through rate is the probability that consumer clicks listing after seeing it in search results. It depends on search position and information visible on the product card, including the title, query relevance, price, and displayed rating. Conversion rate is the probability that click results in purchase. It depends on how well the product satisfies the shoppers needs. These needs include requirements stated directly in the query, such as wattage or device compatibility, as well as requirements implied by the query. Product-page quality and reviews also affect whether click results in purchase. Click-through and conversion rates are defined separately for each querySKU pair, allowing the same product to perform differently across queries. However, even when product is semantically relevant to query and satisfies its stated specifications, the seller cannot determine the querys conversion performance or profitability in advance. To represent this uncertainty, we draw an unobserved conversion multiplier for each querycategory pair when simulated world is created. This multiplier is not visible to sellers and varies across worlds. Sellers must therefore learn keyword performance through observed impressions, clicks, purchases, and advertising costs rather than infer it from semantic relevance alone. (V) Sponsored search advertising. The sponsored-search system provides paid route through which sellers compete for visibility. Sellers submit listing-level bids for individual search queries, and eligible listings compete for four sponsored positions through multi-slot second-price auction. Search traffic is processed in batches during the simulated week, and campaign budgets are depleted as auctions occur. seller may therefore stop participating in later auctions after exhausting its campaign or account budget. Paid and organic traffic subsequently pass through the same click and conversion process. Winning an advertisement does not directly produce sale; it produces an impression whose outcome still depends on the query, listing, search position, and consumer response. Advertising can increase paid sales immediately, and those sales increase the listings recent sales velocity. Higher sales velocity may subsequently improve organic search ranking, leading to more appearances in organic search results, more impressions, and potentially delayed organic sales. The advertising system supports both exploration and exploitation. Under automatic targeting, the platform selects candidate queries for listing. Sellers can then use observed search-term performance to move successful queries into manually managed campaigns or stop spending on unsuccessful ones [Amazon Ads, 2026]. Effective advertising therefore requires an agent to learn query-level performance, adjust bids, allocate budgets, and manage the trade-off between current acquisition costs and possible future organic benefits. (VI) Dynamic competitors. Rival sellers are active market participants rather than static background NPCs. Each competitor follows an operating policy that adapts its decisions to its own market performance. Competitors observe only information available to the corresponding seller, including their sales, margins, sales rank, and advertising reports; they do not observe latent simulator states or other sellers private decisions. Their product specifications, titles, and quality remain fixed after Day-0, while their prices and advertising strategies can change over time. Competitors periodically review their prices using recent sales performance, cost-based price floors, and prevailing market conditions. They also update their advertising strategies by adjusting target 8 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm acquisition costs, query-level bids, campaign budgets, and keyword portfolios according to their margins and observed search-term performance. Consequently, changes in demand or competitive conditions can induce subsequent pricing and advertising responses, making the competitive environment evolve endogenously throughout the simulation. 3.3. The AI Agent Firm The agent firm is set of standing roles, not set of agents assembled for task. Each agent holds one role for the whole run, and handles the work that falls to that function in every period. This inverts the usual multi-agent arrangement, where planner decomposes one goal, spawns sub-agents to carry the tasks, and discards them when the task ends. The structure is not product of the task. It exists first, and work is routed into it. Agents can communicate by email and chat. There is no central scheduler for commucations between colleagues. Each agent manages its own message queue. role definition has two parts. One is the business data the role is responsible for. The other is the set of decision types it may propose, written Ai A. Nothing else is specified. No process, no standard of evidence, no document format, no deadline, no rule for when to escalate. Agents are free to determine their own workflows and coordinate with others. Two properties of this arrangement carry through to the results. First, all roles see the same sanitized business data from the external world model and the firm (Section 3.4). They differ in what they may do, not in what they may know. Second, authority need not follow capability. role can be responsible for the data that reveals problem while the action that resolves it sits with another role. The framework also allows role that approves the proposals of others and holds no action on the world of its own. Agents are constrained to propose actions from fixed catalogue rather than in free text. The external world model can only update the world state with the actions in the catalogue, and other form of decisions cannot be parsed and executed by the external world model. 3.4. Interaction Between the Agent Firm and the External World The agent firm and the external world interact in repeating cycle of fixed length. We call one turn period. At the start of period the world exports filtered copy of its business data. The roles read it, communicate, and propose decisions within their own authority. The approving role accepts or rejects each proposal. At the period boundary the approved decisions and the exogenous events are applied together, and the world model produces the next state. decision approved in one period takes effect only at the start of the next. The company therefore cannot observe an outcome and rewrite it inside the same period. The export passes through several masks, so that no ground truth about the external world model leaks the agents. Whole tables are dropped when they hold latent parameters, internal causal records, or answers. Protected columns are removed from the tables that remain. final audit checks the schema before any file is written, and fails the entire export if anything protected survives. The company has to infer the mechanism from business data alone. The export does no analysis. It contains raw business tables, minimally transformed. Any derived measure has to be defined and computed by the agents, because deciding what to measure is part of the capability under evaluation. Agents from the firm query the export through an isolated read-only environment with SQL and Python tools, which cannot reach the source database. Agents change inputs of the external world model, not results. role may set price, an advertising 9 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm budget, purchase order, or supplier. No role can set demand, profit, or market share. The external world model computes those from the inputs it receives and the state it already holds. price cut, for instance, reaches demand only through the products standing against competing offers, and reaches margin through inventory costs committed in earlier periods. run leaves enough of record to attribute an outcome to single decision. On the world side, what the export withholds is not discarded: the latent parameters and the causal records stay available for scoring. On the firm side, every work item carries its owner and how it entered the queue. Every message carries its sender and recipient, every query the tables it touched, and every decision the role that proposed it and the ruling it received. This separates wrong diagnosis from correct diagnosis whose action was never proposed, and either of those from proposal the approving role declined. Credit assignment to roles and decisions Everything in this loop is recorded. On the world side, what the export withholds is kept rather than discarded, so run can afterwards be checked against the parameters and the causal records that produced it. On the firm side, every task an agent takes on is stored with its owner and its origin, along with every message sent, every query run, and every decision proposed and ruled on. result is therefore attributable to role and to decision, rather than to the firm as whole. The week ends when all employees are idle with no message in flight, or time/step backstop is reached. Measuring time by work rather than by wall clock keeps message ordering reproducible and independent of LLM latency. At the week boundary, the decisions approved by the chief executive (CEO), together with the exogenous events, are applied to the world to produce the next weeks state. 3.5. Fidelity of the Simulated External World Motivation The fidelity of the simulated external world is essential to the validity of MiniCorp as an environment for training and evaluating enterprise agents. Because agent performance is assessed through outcomes generated by the simulated market, realistic-looking snapshots are not sufficient. The markets responses to business decisions, including their direction, dynamics, and trade-offs, must also be consistent with those observed in real markets. Otherwise, agents may learn simulator-specific regularities that do not hold in reality. We refer to this failure mode as simulator overfitting. It does not require an agent to intentionally exploit loophole; it can arise simply because optimization reinforces patterns that exist in the simulator but not in the environment it is intended to represent. In MiniCorp, validating each rule in the external-world model separately does not establish the fidelity of the integrated simulator. These rules govern search ranking, advertising auctions, consumer choice, reviews, inventory, and competitor responses. Market outcomes emerge from their interaction, and their consequences feed back into subsequent rankings and decisions. We therefore evaluate whether the integrated simulator produces end-to-end responses consistent with empirical evidence, rather than stopping at the validation of individual rules. This end-to-end evaluation follows the operational-validation framework described by Sargent [2013] and the empirical-validation framework for agent-based models discussed by Fagiolo et al. [2007]. Our fidelity tests examine whether the simulator reproduces empirical response patterns rather than relying solely on exact point estimates. Matching single empirical estimate is not, by itself, sufficient evidence of fidelity because quantities such as conversion rates, click prices, and price elasticities are highly context-dependent. We therefore treat numerical agreement as supporting evidence when the empirical and simulated settings are comparable, while using the direction, shape, temporal dynamics, distribution, and trade-offs of responses as our primary evaluation criteria. For example, aggressive 10 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm advertising may increase paid sales immediately and improve organic rank over time, while raising acquisition costs and deriving substantial share of incremental sales from competitor displacement rather than market expansion. Such responses create intertemporal and strategic trade-offs that require agents to balance competing business objectives. Pattern-oriented modeling (POM) evaluates an agent-based model by asking whether it can reproduce multiple patterns observed in the real world, rather than judging it against single numerical target [Grimm et al., 2005]. Following this principle, we evaluate MiniCorp against multiple patterns of market response documented in empirical studies. Evaluation of Fidelity Our core methodology is system-level output validation against empirical patterns of market response. For each test, we identify market response documented in empirical studies, reproduce the corresponding intervention or measurement in MiniCorp, and trace its downstream effects. Controlled interventions compare worlds initialized from the same checkpoint and, where applicable, use the same random draws. We evaluate the complete response trajectory, including its direction, temporal ordering, distribution across market participants, and trade-offs among business outcomes. In complex system, matching final outcome is not sufficient; the intermediate responses and feedback effects that produce it must also be consistent with empirical evidence. We therefore focus on response chains and outcomes that were not direct calibration targets, reducing the risk of obtaining the right outcome for the wrong reasons. 4. Experiments and Results 4.1. Experimental Setup The substrate of an AI agent is powered by LLM APIs of the frontier models, GPT-5.6-Sol. Each week proceeds as fixed loop: the world exports data room; agents read it, message one another, and raise proposals; the CEO reviews them; approved decisions are delivered to the world at the end of the week, which then generates the following week. Decisions approved in one week take effect only in the next, lag that prevents the company from observing and rewriting the same outcome within single week. 4.2. Results RQ1: Fidelity of the simulated external world. To what extent does the integrated external world reproduce market responses documented in empirical studies, both in their direct outcomes and in the intermediate pathways through which those outcomes emerge? MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm Table 1: Summary of the main external-world fidelity results. Test Level Key result Why this supports fidelity Immediate price response Outcome 10% price reduction and increase yielded absolute arc elasticities of 2.9 and 3.2, respectively. Temporary discount and price restoration Pathway Temporary stockout Pathway Prices were reduced by 20% for four weeks and then restored to their original levels. Units increased by 71% during the discount, remained 31% above the control for the first four weeks after restoration, and remained 11% above it for the following six weeks. Nearly half of the incremental units were sold after the discount ended. The sales loss persisted after twoweek stockout: 59% of the cumulative unit shortfall occurred after restocking, and sales remained 36% below the control in week 26. Advertising Pathway Ad-attributed units increased by 23 32%, while the organic gain grew from 0.5% to 5.8%. Each additional advertising dollar returned $0.53 in contribution within the observation window, and 84% of incremental units came from competitor displacement. Demand increased when price fell and decreased when price rose. The observed elasticities were also close to the empirical benchmark [Bijmolt et al., 2005]. The observed response followed the pathway: temporary price reduction higher sales higher recent sales velocity more appearances in organic search results more impressions persistently higher sales after price restoration. This pathway is consistent with evidence that past demand can influence subsequent marketplace traffic [Cooprider and Nassiri, 2023; Quaker, 2025]. The stockout produced the opposite pathway: temporary stockout no sales while inventory was unavailable lower recent sales velocity fewer appearances in organic search results after restocking fewer impressions persistently lower sales. This pathway is consistent with evidence that stockouts can reduce future demand and that past demand can influence subsequent marketplace traffic [Anderson et al., 2006; Cooprider and Nassiri, 2023]. The observed response followed the pathway: higher advertising expenditure more paid sales immediately higher recent sales velocity more appearances in organic search results more organic impressions delayed increase in organic sales. This pathway is consistent with Amazons description of how sales and sponsored advertising affect search visibility [Quaker, 2025]. The response also involved an immediate advertising cost but delayed organic benefit, while most incremental sales came at competitors expense rather than from market expansion. We report two levels of fidelity evidence. Outcome-level validation examines whether an intervention produces the expected result, while pathway-level validation additionally examines whether the intermediate responses and their temporal ordering are consistent with empirical evidence. Table 1 summarizes the four such tests. The outcome-level test provides evidence that the simulator produces the expected direct response to business decision. The pathway-level tests further show how these effects propagate over time. 12 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm Temporary discounts and stockouts generate opposite persistent effects through the same sales-history and ranking feedback loop, while advertising produces delayed organic gains together with cost and competitive trade-offs. Because the duration, magnitude, and distribution of these downstream effects were not direct calibration targets, their joint emergence provides system-level fidelity evidence for the default simulator configuration. Robustness across independently initialized worlds remains to be evaluated. RQ2: Organizational realism. To what extent does the agent firm exhibit realistic organizational workflows and operational decision-making? company is not just queue of tasks that get completed. What makes it an organization is where work comes from, how different kinds of work get handled, and who can hand work to whom. We measure all three in the agent firm. The provenance of each work item shows whether the queue is driven by colleagues or by an agents own plan. The process signature of each work category shows whether different kinds of work follow different routines. The delegation structure shows which pairs of roles exchange work, and why. Work is generated by the organization, not by per-agent scripts. In real company, most of what an employee does at the start of the week was not decided by that employee. It carries over from last week, or it arrives because colleague asked. The firms records let us ask whether the same holds here. Each agent works from queue of work items, and every item records where it came from. Table 2 gives the distribution of origins across 30,248 items. Most work in the agent firm is inherited or handed over rather than self-initiated, which is how work arrives in real organization. Only 11% comes from an agents own plan for the week. The largest share, 58%, is carried over from the previous cycle. Another 31% is created by colleagues message or interrupt. Table 2: Provenance of work items.

We classified all 30,248 work items into six operational categories and summarized in Table 3. The clearest pattern lies in the CEO rejection rate: the categories the CEO rejects most often are the ones that spend money. Replenishment and logistics (29%) and advertising and pricing (25%) carry the two highest rejection rates, and both directly commit cash or margin. Quality incidents carry the lowest (13%): placing suspect lot on hold spends nothing and averts losses. Nothing in the CEOs instructions assigns scrutiny in proportion to financial exposure; the allocation emerges from its own judgment. The delegation structure explains the communication pattern. Apart from the CEO, only one pair of roles exchanges work directly at high frequency: Quality Engineering and Supply Chain, in both directions (1,299 exchanges in total, Table 4). The remaining five high-frequency relationships all have the CEO at one end: campaign plans and metric definitions require sign-off, procurement spend requires approval, and tasks are then dispatched downward. Each detected issue therefore requires direct request to Supply Chain to execute the hold, and Supply Chain must report the disposition back, which is why the two directions appear in comparable volumes (704 and 595) and why quality incidents carry the highest message rate in Table 3. This separation of capability from authority routes coordination around the reporting line, pattern characteristic of real organizations. RQ3: Strategic orientation and adaptive market learning. Can explicit long-term strategic guidance induce an LLM agent firm to sustain market exploration despite poor short-term returns, and how does the firm adapt to the market feedback that follows? The paired comparison shows that explicit long-term strategic guidance changed the firms willingness to sacrifice short-term profit to overcome the cold-start problem faced by new products. At launch, the firms listings have little history of clicks, conversions, or sales, while incumbent products have already accumulated these behavioral signals. Because organic search ranking depends on this history, new listings tend to receive low rankings and limited exposure. Early advertising can provide the initial traffic, clicks, and sales needed to improve their position. We compare two setups with the same initial state and market rules. In one run, the CEO, advertising lead, and finance lead were instructed to tolerate short-term advertising losses in order to learn about the market and build toward future organic sales. In the other run, they received no such guidance. The guided firm spent approximately $100 per week from Weeks 212 and about $1,700 over the full 26 weeks, while the unguided firm spent only about $50 in total. Over the same period, the guided firm MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm generated approximately $31,000 in revenue and $3,645 in gross profit before advertising, compared with less than $200 in revenue and $43 in gross profit without guidance. Even after deducting its substantially higher advertising expenditure, the guided firm retained $1,913 in gross profit, whereas the unguided firm recorded $7 loss. Both gross-profit measures exclude refunds, inventory write-offs, and overheads. In this comparison, the guidance sustained investment through weak early returns and helped the firm move beyond its initial cold start, generating enough gross profit on sales to cover its advertising costs over the full period. RQ4: Response to external shocks. Can the agent firm autonomously collaborate to respond to external shocks? Responding to shock takes two things. The firm has to work out which action the situation calls for, and that work has to reach the role that can take it. RQ2 showed the second happens: third of all work arrives from colleague, and the role that detects problem is often not the role that can act on it. Whether any of it changes the final outcome is still the question here. To evaluate the firms ability to react to external shocks, we construct ten scenarios summarized in Table 5 in Appendix, each has an expected route. We evaluate MiniCorp on these ten business situations, each run for eight weekly periods and repeated two times, for total of 20 runs. Table 5 records the action each situation calls for. We score against that action rather than against final profit, since eight weeks is too short for correct repair to pay for itself. run counts as answered when the firm proposes that action and the CEO accepts it. That happens in 11 of 20 runs. In another four the firm does some of what the situation calls for, but not all  (Table 6)  . Collaboration is necessary and helpful The agents exchange 15,970 messages, but the count says nothing about whether any of them changed what the firm did. message can be sent, read, and even quoted in proposal the agent would have made anyway. So for each situation we read the record and ask what the message actually supplied. In four situations colleague plays critical role to solve the problem. Six listings are switched off for being out of stock, and the stock is in fact on hand. The supply lead notices this in week 1. It cannot switch listing back on, so it writes to the demand lead. The demand lead holds that action and reads the same data, but its plan for the week points elsewhere. Without the message, the listings stay off. What the colleague supplies is attention. The data and the authority are already on the demand leads side. In two more situations colleague confirms what the role handling the problem has already worked out. The message helps, though that role could have acted without it. RQ5: Emergent organizational and operational behavior. What emergent behaviors, if any, arose that were not specified in the agents defined roles or responsibilities? No real company runs on predefined script. What an employee does is only loosely determined by their role; the rest requires discretion in judging what matters and developing practices that fit the situation [Park et al., 2023; Akkil et al., 2026]. RQ2 examined how work arises and is routed within the agent firm. Here, we ask whether the firm also generates its own practices. We define emergence along two dimensions. First, the behavior is unspecified. Second, the behavior is not model default. An assistant-trained model brings habits of its own, and behavior that merely expresses them is not the organizations doing. The agents exhibited evasive organizational behavior. In one case, the supply lead identified 19 listings 15 MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm that remained live despite having no stock and asked the demand lead to pause them. The demand lead returned substantive, data-rich replies but never addressed the requested action. It marked the task complete without pausing any listing, creating the appearance of responsiveness without resolving the problem. The agents also developed useful way to improve sales. Besides adjusting advertising and prices, they used search and sales reports to decide how to rewrite product titles. We had not prescribed this sequence of title revisions in the prompts. The agents initiated and developed it during the run. In Week 11 of the guided run, the listing lead found that some queries have better conversion rate, such as usb wall charger and 45w power adapter fast charge for pixel 9. The original SKU title is USB Wall Charger, Pixel 45W USB-C GaN Foldable Charger Block. The agent kept USB Wall Charger in the title and added the wording about fast charging for Pixel 9, and changed the title into USB Wall Charger, 45W Power Adapter Fast Charge for Pixel 9. The new title went live in Week 12. This change brought very positive impact on the orangic search rankings and boosted chargers weekly sales from 91 to 189 units, while its price stayed at $24.95. This operational initiative contrasts with the advertising behavior in RQ3. The unguided firm did not sustain advertising through weak early returns; the guided firm did. In these runs, the agents developed concrete operating practice themselves, while the broader decision to accept short-term losses for future growth still depended on explicit strategic guidance. 5. Conclusion MiniCorp provides closed-loop office simulator that couples persistent agent firm with an evolving market. Its external world is grounded in economic mechanisms and real marketplace data, with end-to-end fidelity evaluated against empirical response patterns. As the firm and market interact over time, MiniCorp generates enterprise records that connect decisions to their business context and consequences. These records also capture emergent organizational and operational behaviors developed by the agents. Checkpointing allows the same situation to be replayed under different decisions, adding counterfactual evidence unavailable in static archives. Together, these features make MiniCorp promising source of scalable, realistic office-work data for evaluating and training models on long-horizon organizational tasks. We envision MiniCorp as scalable source of realistic office-work data for evaluating and training models on long-horizon organizational tasks. More broadly, the framework provides principle that can be extended to additional firms, organizational structures, and industries.
